questions.question: A model has an accuracy of 95% but a recall of 40%. What does this suggest?
options: It’s excellent at identifying all positive cases
It’s missing many actual positive cases
questions.explanation: High accuracy can be misleading in imbalanced datasets. Low recall means many actual positives are missed.

questions.question: You’re building a spam filter. Your model has high precision (98%) but low recall (50%). What’s the likely outcome?
options: Most spam emails are caught, but some legitimate emails are wrongly flagged
Most spam emails are missed, but flagged ones are almost always spam
The model flags too many emails as spam
questions.explanation: High precision means flagged emails are likely spam, but low recall means many spam emails go undetected.

questions.question: A medical tool has recall of 95% and precision of 60%. What does this mean?
options: It rarely misses sick patients but often mislabels healthy ones as sick
questions.explanation: High recall ensures most sick patients are identified, but low precision means many false alarms.

questions.question: A model has perfect precision but very low recall. What kind of behavior is it showing?
options: It’s being very cautious about predicting positives
questions.explanation: Perfect precision means every predicted positive is correct, but low recall means it rarely predicts positives at all.

questions.question: You’re evaluating a model on a highly imbalanced dataset (95% negatives, 5% positives). Which metric is most reliable?
questions.explanation: MCC accounts for all parts of the confusion matrix and is robust to class imbalance.

questions.question:

Actual Negative1090

What does the model’s performance suggest?
options: It’s good at identifying positives and negatives
questions.explanation: High true positives and true negatives, with relatively few errors. Accuracy = 80%; Recall = 70%.

questions.question: What does a recall of 70% and precision of 87.5% tell you?
options: The model is cautious and misses many positives
The model mislabels negatives as positives
The model catches most positives and is usually correct when it does
questions.explanation: Recall = 70%; Precision = 87.5%. The model is effective at identifying positives and minimizing false alarms.

questions.question:
A fraud detection model produces the following confusion matrix:

Predicted FraudPredicted Legit
Actual Fraud3070
Actual Legit1090

What does this model’s behavior suggest?
options: It catches most fraud cases but mislabels many legitimate users
It balances precision and recall well
It avoids flagging legitimate users but catches most fraud
It is cautious about flagging fraud and misses many actual cases
questions.explanation: Recall is low (30%), meaning most fraud cases are missed. Precision is moderate (75%), and false positives are relatively few. The model is conservative in flagging fraud, prioritizing caution over coverage.

questions.question: Two models have the same accuracy of 85%, but one has an MCC of 0.82 and the other has an MCC of 0.35. What does this tell you?
options: The model with lower MCC is better at identifying positives
Accuracy is all that matters, so they are equally good
The model with higher MCC has more balanced predictions
MCC only matters for multi-class problems
questions.explanation: MCC reflects the balance between true and false predictions across both classes. A higher MCC indicates better overall correlation between predictions and actual labels, even if accuracy is the same.
